package_info.package_manager: unknown (likely npm or direct binary distribution)
package_info.package_versions: unknown (affected version in 2021 supply chain attack)
package_info.why_malicious: The package was malicious because attackers tampered with the artifact to include code that harvested sensitive build environment variables (such as credentials and tokens) and exfiltrated them to a third-party server. This modification was not part of the legitimate functionality and directly enabled credential theft.

execution_context.trigger: at runtime (when the uploader is executed in CI/CD or build environments)
execution_context.file_location: main uploader script (e.g., bash-uploader.sh or equivalent entrypoint)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code enumerates all environment variables, filters for those containing sensitive keywords (TOKEN, KEY, SECRET), and sends their names and values via HTTP POST to a hardcoded third-party server, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code actively searches for environment variables likely to contain secrets and exfiltrates them to an external, attacker-controlled server. This is a direct credential theft technique and is never part of legitimate uploader functionality.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate uploader should only transmit user-specified artifacts to trusted endpoints and should not access or transmit environment variables, especially those containing secrets, to untrusted domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate telemetry or error reporting might send non-sensitive environment data (such as OS version or build ID) to a trusted endpoint, but never secrets, tokens, or credentials, and never to a hardcoded, non-customer domain.
key_indicators: Enumeration of environment variables with sensitive keywords (TOKEN, KEY, SECRET)
Use of 'curl' or similar utilities to send data to a hardcoded external URL
Presence of exfiltration logic in the main uploader script
No user interaction or consent for transmitting environment data

attack_chain.action: Attacker gains access to the artifact creation process and injects malicious code into the uploader script.
attack_chain.leads_to: Distribution of the compromised artifact to customers

attack_chain.action: Customers download and execute the compromised uploader in their CI/CD or build environments.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of malicious code in trusted environments

attack_chain.action: Malicious code enumerates environment variables for secrets and exfiltrates them to the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credential theft and potential further compromise

behavioral_signatures: Uploader scripts or binaries accessing environment variables with sensitive keywords such as TOKEN, KEY, or SECRET
Unexpected network requests to hardcoded, non-customer domains during artifact upload or build processes
Uploader tools transmitting data not related to the intended artifact, especially environment variable contents
file_indicators: Uploader scripts containing the sequence 'env | grep -E' and 'curl' or similar exfiltration logic
Presence of hardcoded external URLs (e.g., https://malicious.example.com/collect) in uploader code
network_indicators: HTTP/HTTPS POST requests to domains not associated with the legitimate service, such as https://malicious.example.com/collect
Outbound connections from CI/CD runners or build environments to unknown or suspicious endpoints
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor uploader and build scripts for code that accesses environment variables and sends data to external servers. Use static analysis to flag scripts containing both environment variable enumeration (e.g., 'env | grep') and network exfiltration logic (e.g., 'curl' or 'wget' to non-customer domains). Monitor network traffic from build environments for unexpected outbound POST requests, especially to unrecognized or hardcoded domains. Validate artifact provenance and signatures to ensure only trusted, untampered artifacts are used in CI/CD pipelines.
